topics.example: Adorno critiqued commercial pop music as repetitive formula designed for mindless consumption; Birmingham cultural theorists showed how punk subcultures took commodified clothing and subverted it into anti-establishment protest.
topics.understandMore: Popular culture can mean: folk culture produced by the people, mass culture manufactured by corporate media, or whatever is excluded from the high culture canon. Cultural Studies insists audiences actively negotiate media texts rather than passively submitting to them.
topics.commonConfusion: The Frankfurt School saw mass culture as total ideological manipulation from above; Cultural Studies recognizes dominant ideology but insists on audience resistance and semiotic agency from below.
topics.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 44; Question Bank, p. 71, 72, 75

topics.title: Cultural Consumption and Active Resistance (Hall, Fiske)
topics.coreIdea: Cultural theorists shifted focus from the production of cultural commodities to their consumption. John Fiske in 'Understanding Popular Culture' (1989) distinguished the financial economy (where corporations sell goods for profit) from the cultural economy (where consumers make their own subversive meanings and pleasures). Drawing on Michel de Certeau, consumers are viewed as 'textual poachers' who tactically re-appropriate mass culture.
topics.vivaAnswer: Consumption in cultural studies is an active, productive practice rather than passive absorption. Consumers 'poach' corporate commodities, rewriting their meanings to create unauthorized pleasures and subcultural identities.
topics.example: Youth subcultures turning safety pins, torn jeans, or military boots into symbols of anti-establishment rebellion illustrates active consumption subverting the original corporate utility.
topics.understandMore: Fiske argued that capitalism cannot control how commodities are used once they enter the street. However, critical cultural theorists note that consumer capitalism frequently re-incorporates and monetizes subcultural rebellion, turning anti-fashion into retail trends.
topics.commonConfusion: Consuming is not merely buying an item at a store; cultural consumption is the semiotic process of using, interpreting, and imbuing commodities with lived personal meaning.
topics.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 44-45; Question Bank, p. 72, 83

topics.title: Representation and the Encoding/Decoding Model (Stuart Hall)
topics.coreIdea: In 'Representation' (1997) and his 1973 model, Stuart Hall established that representation connects meaning and language to culture. He outlined three approaches: reflective (language reflects reality), intentional (language expresses authorial intent), and constructionist (language constructs meaning using cultural codes). His Encoding/Decoding model posits that media texts are encoded with a 'preferred meaning' but decoded through three audience positions: dominant-hegemonic, negotiated, or oppositional.
topics.vivaAnswer: Stuart Hall argued that meaning is constructed through representational codes. His Encoding/Decoding model identifies three decoding stances: the dominant-hegemonic reading (accepting the preferred message), the negotiated reading (adapting it to local conditions), and the oppositional reading (rejecting and decoding it within an alternative framework).
topics.example: When watching a government broadcast urging wage freezes to fight inflation: a CEO adopts the dominant-hegemonic reading (agreeing completely); a middle manager takes a negotiated reading (accepting overall need but disputing its fairness to their branch); a trade unionist takes an oppositional reading (decoding the broadcast as an attack on working-class livelihoods).
topics.understandMore: Hall demonstrated the constructionist approach using Velázquez's painting 'Las Meninas' (following Foucault), showing how representation constructs unstable subject-positions where the viewer is simultaneously spectator and observed. Hall divided constructionism into semiotic (Saussure, Barthes) and discursive (Foucault) variants.
topics.commonConfusion: The message sent is not automatically the message received: encoding and decoding are asymmetrical moments separated by social codes and audience agency.
topics.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 45-46; Question Bank, p. 69, 71, 74

questions.question: What is defamiliarization (ostranenie) in Russian Formalism?
questions.directAnswer: The artistic technique of making familiar objects strange to disrupt automatic perception.
questions.vivaAnswer: Defamiliarization, introduced by Viktor Shklovsky as 'ostranenie', is art's technique of presenting ordinary things in unfamiliar ways. It breaks the dulling habit of automatic perception, forcing the reader to truly experience and see the object rather than simply recognizing it.
keyPoints: Coined by Viktor Shklovsky in 'Art as Technique' (1917)
Russian term 'ostranenie' means 'making strange'
Counters habitual, automated perception
Makes forms difficult and prolongs the perceptual experience
questions.explanation: Shklovsky argued that in daily life, perception becomes automated—we swallow things whole without really seeing them. The purpose of art is to impart the sensation of things as they are perceived and not as they are known, prolonging perception because the process of perceiving is an aesthetic end in itself.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 3-4; Question Bank, p. 49

questions.question: How does defamiliarization differ from foregrounding?
questions.directAnswer: Defamiliarization is the psychological/perceptual effect of making the familiar strange, while foregrounding is the specific linguistic technique of making textual features prominent.
questions.vivaAnswer: Defamiliarization is a perceptual and psychological effect where art makes us see the world afresh, as proposed by Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky. Foregrounding, formulated by the Prague School, is the specific linguistic mechanism—such as deviation or parallelism—that makes the language itself stand out against ordinary speech.
keyPoints: Defamiliarization: perceptual/aesthetic end (Shklovsky)
Foregrounding: linguistic means/mechanics (Prague School, Mukařovský)
Foregrounding achieves defamiliarization through linguistic deviation and parallelism
questions.explanation: Foregrounding is the technique; defamiliarization is the result. When a poet disrupts standard syntax (foregrounding), the reader's automated response is broken, forcing them to perceive the world and the text newly (defamiliarization).
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 4; Question Bank, p. 49

questions.question: Give a literary example of defamiliarization from Viktor Shklovsky's writings.
questions.directAnswer: Tolstoy's story 'Kholstomer', narrated from the perspective of a horse puzzled by private property.
questions.vivaAnswer: Shklovsky cites Leo Tolstoy's story 'Kholstomer', which is narrated by a horse. The horse expresses profound confusion over human phrases like 'my horse' or 'my land', thereby defamiliarizing the conventional human concept of private property and exposing its absurdity.
keyPoints: Tolstoy's 'Kholstomer' narrated by an animal
Exposes private ownership as an unnatural social construct
Tolstoy also describes flogging without using the word 'flog', describing physical stripping and striking
questions.explanation: By describing human social customs through the innocent, unconditioned gaze of a horse, Tolstoy strips away cultural assumptions, enabling readers to perceive human greed and ownership as bizarre and unnatural.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 3-4; Question Bank, p. 49, 53

questions.question: What were the primary criticisms directed against Russian Formalism?
questions.directAnswer: Critics attacked Formalism for treating literature as an isolated verbal machine and ignoring historical, social, and political contexts.
questions.vivaAnswer: Russian Formalism was heavily criticized, especially by Marxist theorists like Leon Trotsky and Mikhail Bakhtin, for isolating literature from history, politics, and human life. By reducing art to pure formal devices and verbal games, Formalism was seen as sterile, socially irresponsible, and politically blind.
keyPoints: Accused of aesthetic isolationism and 'art for art's sake'
Leon Trotsky's critique in 'Literature and Revolution' (1924)
Bakhtin School criticized its failure to consider social dialogue and ideology
Neglects the author's social reality and the reader's historical situatedness
questions.explanation: Soviet cultural authorities in the late 1920s suppressed Formalism because it refused to evaluate literature according to socialist ideological utility, insisting that form determines content rather than social reality.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 3; Question Bank, p. 53, 54

questions.question: Which linguists and poets are most closely associated with the concept of foregrounding?
questions.directAnswer: Jan Mukařovský of the Prague Linguistic Circle and the Russian Futurist poet Vladimir Mayakovsky.
questions.vivaAnswer: Foregrounding was theoretically formulated by Jan Mukařovský and Roman Jakobson of the Prague Linguistic Circle in the 1930s. The concept is poetically exemplified by Vladimir Mayakovsky, whose radical Russian Futurist poetry deliberately foregrounded language through abrupt rhythms, neologisms, and visual line breaks.
keyPoints: Jan Mukařovský (Czech aesthetician/linguist, Prague School)
Roman Jakobson (co-founder of Prague Linguistic Circle)
Vladimir Mayakovsky (Russian Futurist poet who applied it in practice)
questions.explanation: Mukařovský demonstrated that poetic language is defined by the maximum foregrounding of the utterance, pushing ordinary communicative function into the background.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 4-5; Question Bank, p. 49, 50

questions.question: What are the two primary linguistic methods through which foregrounding is achieved?
questions.directAnswer: Deviation (violating linguistic norms) and Parallelism (introducing unexpected regularities).
questions.vivaAnswer: Foregrounding is achieved primarily through deviation and parallelism. Deviation breaks grammatical, phonological, or semantic rules to surprise the reader, while parallelism creates heightened, unexpected symmetry and repetition in rhythm, sound, or sentence structure.
keyPoints: Linguistic deviation: breaking standard syntactic, lexical, or phonological rules (e.g., e.e. cummings)
Parallelism: creating patterned repetitions and symmetries (e.g., alliteration, meter, rhyme)
Both draw attention to the verbal texture itself
questions.explanation: In everyday speech, language is transparent—we look through words to get the information. Foregrounding makes language opaque, so the reader contemplates the physical medium of language itself.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 4; Question Bank, p. 49, 50

questions.question: What is Practical Criticism as pioneered by I.A. Richards?
questions.directAnswer: An empirical method of close reading that analyzes texts without authorial names, dates, or biographical information.
questions.vivaAnswer: Practical Criticism, pioneered by I.A. Richards at Cambridge University in 1929, is a critical method that evaluates poems purely on their internal textual evidence. Richards gave students anonymous poems without author names or historical dates to test their ability to interpret the words on the page directly.
keyPoints: Developed by I.A. Richards at Cambridge ('Practical Criticism', 1929)
Stripped texts of author, title, and historical context
Exposed widespread misreading and reliance on preconceptions
Laid the pedagogical foundation for Anglo-American close reading
questions.explanation: Richards discovered that even advanced Cambridge literature students misread poems drastically when deprived of authorial prestige, proving that literary education had relied on biographical reverence rather than actual close reading skills.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 5; Question Bank, p. 51, 54

questions.question: What is the difference between the Intentional Fallacy and the Affective Fallacy in New Criticism?
questions.directAnswer: The Intentional Fallacy confuses the poem with its author's intention; the Affective Fallacy confuses the poem with its emotional effect on the reader.
questions.vivaAnswer: Formulated by W.K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley, the Intentional Fallacy is the mistaken belief that a text's meaning is determined by the author's private design. The Affective Fallacy is the opposing error of judging a text's value by the emotional impact or psychological impressions it produces in the reader.
keyPoints: Coined by W.K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley (1946/1949)
Intentional Fallacy: judging art by the author's intended message (origin)
Affective Fallacy: judging art by the reader's emotional reactions (destination)
Both fallacies distract from the poem itself as an objective verbal icon
questions.explanation: New Critics argued that once a poem is written, it belongs to the public and the linguistic system. The critic must focus strictly on the autonomous text—neither psychoanalyzing the author's mind nor charting the reader's tears.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 5-6; Question Bank, p. 51, 54

questions.question: What is Cleanth Brooks's 'Heresy of Paraphrase'?
questions.directAnswer: The false assumption that a poem's core meaning can be summarized in a prose statement without destroying its aesthetic essence.
questions.vivaAnswer: Cleanth Brooks argued in 'The Well Wrought Urn' (1947) that reducing a poem to a prose summary is a critical 'heresy'. A poem is an organic whole where form and content are inseparable; its meaning emerges through complex internal tensions, ironies, and paradoxes that evaporate the moment it is paraphrased.
keyPoints: Formulated by Cleanth Brooks in 'The Well Wrought Urn' (1947)
Form and content cannot be divided in genuine poetry
Paraphrase extracts a mere abstract proposition, missing the poetic tension
Poetic meaning is enacted by the structure, not stated by a prose thesis
questions.explanation: For New Critics, a poem does not simply point to a message like a signpost; it embodies its meaning through its precise rhythmic, metaphorical, and paradoxical architecture.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 5-6; Question Bank, p. 51, 52

questions.question: How did William Empson extend Practical Criticism in 'Seven Types of Ambiguity'?
questions.directAnswer: By demonstrating that literary language is intrinsically multifaceted, conveying multiple simultaneous meanings rather than a single fixed definition.
questions.vivaAnswer: William Empson, a student of I.A. Richards, published 'Seven Types of Ambiguity' (1930) to show that verbal ambiguity is not a flaw in poetry, but its greatest aesthetic virtue. He cataloged how great poets deliberately exploit linguistic double-meanings, puns, and grammatical uncertainties to enrich textual resonance.
keyPoints: William Empson (student of I.A. Richards, 1930)
Ambiguity is an artistic asset rather than a linguistic defect
Reveals seven escalating degrees of verbal complexity in English literature
questions.explanation: Empson proved that poetic language thrives on layered overtones, where contradictory interpretations can coexist harmoniously within the same line of verse.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 5; Question Bank, p. 51

questions.question: What is a linguistic sign according to Ferdinand de Saussure?
questions.directAnswer: A two-sided psychological unit uniting a signifier (sound-image) and a signified (mental concept).
questions.vivaAnswer: Ferdinand de Saussure defined a linguistic sign as a two-part entity combining a signifier—the acoustic or written sound-image—and a signified—the mental concept it evokes. The sign does not link a word directly to a physical object, but links a sensory form to a mental concept.
keyPoints: Saussure's 'Course in General Linguistics' (1916)
Signifier (signifiant): the material/acoustic form
Signified (signifié): the mental concept or meaning
Two sides of the same coin; inseparable in language
questions.explanation: Saussure stressed that the signified is not a physical object in the real world (which is the referent), but an abstract mental concept shared by speakers of a linguistic community.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 7-8; Question Bank, p. 50, 53

questions.question: Why did Saussure insist that the linguistic sign is arbitrary and relational?
questions.directAnswer: Because there is no natural link between sound and concept, and meaning is established purely through difference from other signs.
questions.vivaAnswer: Saussure argued the sign is arbitrary because no natural connection exists between the sound-sequence 'tree' and the concept of a tree—proven by the fact that French uses 'arbre'. Furthermore, signs are purely relational: meaning exists not through inherent qualities, but through negative differences ('in language there are only differences without positive terms').
keyPoints: Arbitrariness: no natural or motivated link between signifier and signified
Conventionality: meaning depends on socially agreed linguistic codes
Relational value (valeur): a sign is defined by what it is not in the system
questions.explanation: A traffic light's red signal means 'stop' not because red has an inherent essence of halting, but because it is conventionally distinguished from green ('go') and yellow ('caution') within a differential system.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 7-8; Question Bank, p. 53, 67

questions.question: What is the distinction between the syntagmatic axis and the paradigmatic axis?
questions.directAnswer: The syntagmatic axis is the horizontal chain of combination; the paradigmatic axis is the vertical pool of selection.
questions.vivaAnswer: The syntagmatic axis is the horizontal line of combination, where words are arranged sequentially in a sentence according to grammatical rules. The paradigmatic axis is the vertical dimension of selection, representing the pool of interchangeable alternative words that could fit into a specific position.
keyPoints: Syntagmatic axis: combination in praesentia (words co-present in linear sequence)
Paradigmatic axis: selection in absentia (words chosen from an associative group)
Jakobson linked syntagm to metonymy and paradigm to metaphor
questions.explanation: In 'The sailor navigated the ship', 'sailor' is chosen from a vertical paradigm (captain, crewman, soldier) and joined along a horizontal syntagm with 'navigated' and 'the ship'.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 8; Question Bank, p. 53

questions.question: What are binary oppositions and how did Claude Lévi-Strauss utilize them?
questions.directAnswer: Contrasting pairs of concepts used by the human mind to organize cultural meaning and resolve structural contradictions.
questions.vivaAnswer: Binary oppositions are pairs of mutually exclusive, contrasting terms (e.g., raw/cooked, nature/culture, male/female). Anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss demonstrated that human cultures structure myths worldwide around these binary poles, using mythic narratives to mediate and resolve underlying social anxieties.
keyPoints: Core concept of structuralist anthropology and linguistics
Lévi-Strauss applied Jakobson's phonological contrasts to human culture
Myths function as cultural machines to mediate deep binary conflicts
questions.explanation: In 'The Raw and the Cooked', Lévi-Strauss showed that the transformation of raw food into cooked food represents culture overcoming wild nature, a universal symbolic threshold across all human mythologies.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 8-9; Question Bank, p. 50, 53

questions.question: What are Northrop Frye's four 'mythoi' in archetypal criticism?
questions.directAnswer: Comedy (Spring), Romance (Summer), Tragedy (Autumn), and Irony/Satire (Winter).
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Anatomy of Criticism' (1957), Northrop Frye classified all Western literature into four master narrative patterns called 'mythoi', mapped onto the four seasons: Comedy represents Spring (renewal and birth); Romance represents Summer (heroic quest and fulfillment); Tragedy represents Autumn (the fall and death of the hero); and Irony/Satire represents Winter (defeat, disillusionment, and darkness).
keyPoints: Northrop Frye's 'Anatomy of Criticism' (1957)
Spring / Comedy: renewal, triumph of youth, marriage
Summer / Romance: adventure, quest, wish-fulfillment
Autumn / Tragedy: hubris, inevitable catastrophe, death
Winter / Irony & Satire: realism, absurdity, trapped human anti-hero
questions.explanation: Frye argued that literary plots are not isolated inventions, but cyclical movements within a unified archetypal cosmos derived from solar and seasonal myths.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 9-10; Question Bank, p. 50, 51, 75

questions.question: Distinguish between the mythos of spring and the mythos of autumn according to Frye.
questions.directAnswer: Spring (Comedy) moves from social restriction to renewal and festivity; Autumn (Tragedy) moves from order and prosperity to catastrophic downfall and isolation.
questions.vivaAnswer: The mythos of spring (Comedy) is a narrative of resurrection and social integration: young lovers overcome tyrannical paternal obstacles to establish a renewed society, traditionally sealed by a wedding. In contrast, the mythos of autumn (Tragedy) depicts the descent of an exceptional protagonist from peak prosperity into irreversible disaster, isolation, and death due to an error or fate.
keyPoints: Spring (Comedy): upward trajectory, social renewal, integration, marriage
Autumn (Tragedy): downward trajectory, individual isolation, catastrophe, sacrifice
Represents the natural cycle of birth (spring) and dying (autumn)
questions.explanation: While Shakespeare's 'As You Like It' moves into the green world of Arden to renew society (Spring), 'King Lear' tears apart an orderly kingdom and ends in desolate sacrifice on a blasted heath (Autumn).
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 9-10; Question Bank, p. 51, 75

questions.question: How do narratologists distinguish between 'story' (fabula) and 'plot' (syuzhet)?
questions.directAnswer: Story (fabula) is the chronological sequence of events; Plot (syuzhet) is the specific artistic arrangement of those events in the narrative.
questions.vivaAnswer: Originating in Russian Formalism and refined in narratology, 'story' (fabula) is the raw, chronological timeline of events as they happened in causal sequence. 'Plot' (syuzhet) is the aesthetic arrangement and discursive presentation of those events within the text, utilizing flashbacks, flash-forwards, ellipses, and reordering for artistic effect.
keyPoints: Fabula (story): chronological, causal chain of raw events
Syuzhet (plot): artistic, textured narrative organization on the page
Plots can start in medias res, reorder events, or conceal pivotal actions
questions.explanation: In a mystery novel, the fabula begins with the murderer planning and committing the crime; the syuzhet begins with the detective discovering the corpse hours later, reconstructing the fabula retrospectively.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 10; Question Bank, p. 50, 54, 55

questions.question: What is Tzvetan Todorov's five-stage formula for narrative equilibrium?
questions.directAnswer: Equilibrium, Disruption, Recognition of disruption, Repair/Resolution, and New Equilibrium.
questions.vivaAnswer: Tzvetan Todorov argued in 'Grammar of the Decameron' that all narratives cycle through five structural states: 1) initial equilibrium, 2) disruption by an external force or villain, 3) recognition that disruption has occurred, 4) an attempt to repair the damage, and 5) the establishment of a transformed, new equilibrium.
keyPoints: Tzvetan Todorov (structuralist narratologist)
5 stages: Initial equilibrium -> Disruption -> Recognition -> Repair -> New equilibrium
Narrative is a movement from one state of stability to another via crisis
questions.explanation: The final equilibrium is never a simple return to the starting point; characters have changed, lessons have been learned, and the social structure is reconfigured.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 10; Question Bank, p. 54

questions.question: Who identified thirty-one narrative functions across Russian folktales?
questions.directAnswer: Vladimir Propp in 'Morphology of the Folktale' (1928).
questions.vivaAnswer: Vladimir Propp identified thirty-one immutable narrative functions (such as 'absentation', 'interdiction', 'villainy', and 'departure') in his 1928 study 'Morphology of the Folktale'. He showed that while character names change, their narrative functions and roles (spheres of action) remain constant across all traditional wonder-tales.
keyPoints: Vladimir Propp ('Morphology of the Folktale', 1928)
31 narrative functions executed in predictable sequence
7 character spheres of action: Hero, Villain, Donor, Helper, Princess/Father, Dispatcher, False Hero
questions.explanation: Propp's morphology demonstrated that complex folklore is generated by a surprisingly simple, closed structural system, serving as a direct precursor to modern narratology.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 10; Question Bank, p. 54

questions.question: What does Roland Barthes mean by 'myth' in 'Mythologies'?
questions.directAnswer: A second-order semiotic system that turns contingent, historical bourgeois ideologies into seemingly natural facts.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Mythologies' (1957), Roland Barthes defined myth as a second-order semiological system. A sign produced at the first level of language (denotation) becomes the mere signifier for a secondary ideological meaning (connotation). Myth depoliticizes culture by making socially constructed, bourgeois values appear natural, universal, and innocent.
keyPoints: Roland Barthes's 'Mythologies' (1957)
Second-order signification: sign becomes signifier for mythic signified
Naturalizes ideology: turns history into 'nature'
Conceals ruling-class power beneath an innocent appearance
questions.explanation: Barthes emphasized that myth does not deny things; it purifies them, making them innocent and giving them a natural, eternal justification.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 10-11; Question Bank, p. 50, 52

questions.question: Explain Barthes's famous example of the Paris Match magazine cover.
questions.directAnswer: A photo of a Black soldier saluting the French flag denotes a soldier saluting, but connotes the myth of French imperial benevolence and unity.
questions.vivaAnswer: On the cover of Paris Match, a young Black soldier in French uniform salutes the French flag. At the first level (denotation), it is simply a photograph of a Black soldier saluting. At the second level (myth/connotation), it functions as an ideological signifier promoting French imperial greatness, suggesting that all subjects proudly and loyally serve the French empire, thereby neutralizing anti-colonial critique.
keyPoints: First level (denotation): Black soldier saluting the tricolor flag
Second level (myth): French imperial unity, colonial legitimacy, and racial harmony
Serves to justify French colonialism during the Algerian war era
questions.explanation: Barthes demonstrated how mass media images naturalize political propaganda, convincing French citizens that colonial empire is a noble, harmonious family rather than a violent military occupation.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 11; Question Bank, p. 50, 52

questions.question: What is the 'hermeneutic circle' in text interpretation?
questions.directAnswer: The interpretive principle that the part can only be understood in relation to the whole, and the whole through its parts.
questions.vivaAnswer: The hermeneutic circle is a fundamental principle of interpretation: one cannot understand the meaning of any individual word or passage without grasping the context of the entire work, yet understanding the whole work is only possible through comprehending its individual parts. It forms an ongoing, deepening spiral of understanding.
keyPoints: Associated with Schleiermacher, Dilthey, and Gadamer
Understanding moves dialectically between part and whole
Not a vicious circularity, but a productive ontological process
Reader brings pre-understanding that is modified as reading proceeds
questions.explanation: In reading a novel, each sentence adjusts our comprehension of the complete theme, while our emerging grasp of the theme simultaneously reinterprets every earlier sentence.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 12-13; Question Bank, p. 70

questions.question: What did Hans-Georg Gadamer mean by the 'fusion of horizons'?
questions.directAnswer: The interpretive dialogue where the historical horizon of the text and the present horizon of the reader merge into new understanding.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Truth and Method' (1960), Hans-Georg Gadamer argued that genuine interpretation is a 'fusion of horizons' (Horizontverschmelzung). An interpreter cannot escape their own historical situation and prejudices; rather, reading is an open dialogue where the historical horizon of the past text merges with the present horizon of the interpreter, creating fresh meaning.
keyPoints: Hans-Georg Gadamer ('Truth and Method', 1960)
Rejects the illusion of completely objective, detached historical reading
Prejudices (Vorurteile) are necessary conditions for understanding
Interpretation is a dynamic conversation between past and present
questions.explanation: Gadamer proved that when we read ancient texts like Homer or the Bible, we cannot reconstruct the author's original mind; instead, we bring the past into living dialogue with our contemporary consciousness.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 12-13; Question Bank, p. 70

questions.question: How does Roman Ingarden's phenomenology describe literary works?
questions.directAnswer: As intentional schematic objects filled with 'spots of indeterminacy' that require reader concretization.
questions.vivaAnswer: Polish phenomenologist Roman Ingarden argued in 'The Literary Work of Art' (1931) that a literary text is an 'intentional object' possessing a schematic structure. Because texts cannot describe every detail of reality, they contain inevitable 'spots of indeterminacy' (Unbestimmtheitsstellen) which the reader must actively fill in and complete (concretize) in their consciousness.
keyPoints: Roman Ingarden ('The Literary Work of Art', 1931)
Spots of indeterminacy (Unbestimmtheitsstellen) inherent in all writing
Concretization: reader actively visualizes and completes unwritten details
Direct precursor to Wolfgang Iser's reader-response theory
questions.explanation: A text provides skeletal cues; the reader's imaginative consciousness fleshes out the characters, scenery, and implicit connections into a living aesthetic object.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 13; Question Bank, p. 70

questions.question: What is Hans Robert Jauss's 'horizon of expectations'?
questions.directAnswer: The shared set of cultural criteria, genre norms, and assumptions readers hold when encountering a text in a given era.
questions.vivaAnswer: Hans Robert Jauss introduced the 'horizon of expectations' (Erwartungshorizont) in his Aesthetics of Reception. It refers to the shared system of literary conventions, cultural beliefs, and aesthetic criteria that readers in a specific historical moment use to interpret and evaluate a new literary work.
keyPoints: Hans Robert Jauss (Aesthetics of Reception, Constance School)
Erwartungshorizont: collective historical mindset of a reading public
Determines how a text is understood and evaluated at publication
Changes over time, explaining shifting literary reputations across history
questions.explanation: Because horizons of expectations evolve across generations, Shakespeare or Milton means something very different to twenty-first-century readers than to seventeenth-century audiences.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 13-14; Question Bank, p. 70, 71

questions.question: What is 'aesthetic distance' in Jauss's Reception Theory?
questions.directAnswer: The gap between the reader's existing expectations and the challenge presented by a new literary work.
questions.vivaAnswer: Aesthetic distance is the gap between a society's established horizon of expectations and the innovative demands of a new text. Works that conform completely to expectations have zero distance and are merely entertaining or 'culinary', while masterpieces rupture existing expectations, initially provoking shock or rejection before gradually creating a new horizon.
keyPoints: Measures the artistic originality and value of a text
Low distance: trivial, commercial entertainment confirming clichés
High distance: avant-garde art that shatters conventions and transforms taste
questions.explanation: Flaubert's 'Madame Bovary' had massive aesthetic distance in 1857 because it refused to provide a moralizing narrator to condemn Emma's adultery, causing a legal prosecution before becoming an acclaimed literary benchmark.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 14; Question Bank, p. 70, 71

questions.question: What is Wolfgang Iser's concept of the 'implied reader'?
questions.directAnswer: The hypothetical reader role pre-structured into the text's linguistic and narrative design.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'The Implied Reader' (1974), Wolfgang Iser defined the implied reader not as an actual, flesh-and-blood individual, but as a textual construct. It is the role pre-structured into the narrative itself, embodying all the orientations, competencies, and interpretive invitations necessary for the text to realize its aesthetic potential.
keyPoints: Wolfgang Iser ('The Implied Reader', 'The Act of Reading')
Textual condition and role, not an empirical living reader
Pre-structures how the actual reader must assemble textual clues
Contrast with actual reader (individual psychological person)
questions.explanation: Every text anticipates a certain kind of reader through its vocabulary, allusions, and pacing; the implied reader is that ideal textual mechanism.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 14-15; Question Bank, p. 70, 71

questions.question: What role do 'gaps' or 'blanks' (Leerstellen) play in Iser's reading process?
questions.directAnswer: They stimulate the reader's imagination to connect unstated narrative relationships and actively produce meaning.
questions.vivaAnswer: Iser argued that literary texts are full of structural 'blanks' or gaps (Leerstellen)—unwritten pauses, unstated motives, and unexplained shifts between perspectives. These gaps stimulate the reader's imagination, compelling the reader to formulate hypotheses, connect fragmented scenes, and actively co-create the aesthetic work.
keyPoints: Leerstellen (gaps/blanks) are essential catalysts for active reading
Reader travels along a 'wandering viewpoint'
Meaning is produced in the interactive space between text and reader
questions.explanation: If a text explained everything completely and unambiguously, it would be boring and dead; it is the gaps that make reading an engaging, dynamic partnership.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 14-15; Question Bank, p. 70, 71

questions.question: What did Stanley Fish mean by 'interpretive communities'?
questions.directAnswer: Shared institutional strategies and interpretive norms that determine how groups of readers construct textual meaning.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Is There a Text in This Class?' (1980), Stanley Fish argued that meaning does not reside in the text or in the private psyche of an isolated individual reader, but is produced by 'interpretive communities'. These are communities of readers who share institutional interpretive conventions, determining in advance what counts as a valid reading.
keyPoints: Stanley Fish ('Is There a Text in This Class?', 1980)
Radical reader-response: text has no objective meaning outside interpretation
Interpretive communities prevent chaotic subjectivism through shared social codes
questions.explanation: A group of academic literary scholars reads a poem through modern critical conventions, while a religious congregation reads the same words as sacred prophecy; both belong to distinct interpretive communities.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 15; Question Bank, p. 70

questions.question: How does J.L. Austin distinguish between performative and constative utterances?
questions.directAnswer: Constatives state facts and are true or false; performatives execute an action and are felicitous or infelicitous.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'How to Do Things with Words' (1962), J.L. Austin distinguished constative utterances—statements that describe reality and can be judged true or false ('The snow is white')—from performative utterances—statements that perform an action in the very act of being uttered ('I promise to pay you', 'I name this ship'). Performatives do not describe; they act.
keyPoints: J.L. Austin ('How to Do Things with Words', 1962)
Constative: descriptive, fact-stating, truth-evaluable (true/false)
Performative: action-executing, alters reality, evaluable by felicity conditions
questions.explanation: Performative statements require proper social conventions, authorized speakers, and sincere intentions to be 'happy' (felicitous); if conventions are violated, they misfire.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 15-16; Question Bank, p. 70

questions.question: Differentiate between locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts.
questions.directAnswer: Locutionary is the act of saying something; Illocutionary is the action done in saying it; Perlocutionary is the effect caused by saying it.
questions.vivaAnswer: Austin divided every speech act into three simultaneous dimensions: 1) the Locutionary act is the literal act of uttering meaningful words; 2) the Illocutionary act is the conventional action performed in saying those words (e.g., warning, ordering, promising); and 3) the Perlocutionary act is the psychological consequence or effect produced on the listener (e.g., frightening, persuading, amusing).
keyPoints: Locution: the physical phonetic and semantic utterance ('Shoot her!')
Illocution: the intended social force or act (ordering the listener to shoot)
Perlocution: the actual effect achieved (persuading or terrifying the listener)
questions.explanation: In literary dialogue and drama, playwrights structure tension not merely through locutions (words spoken), but through illocutionary confrontations where characters threaten, plead, and command.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 15-16; Question Bank, p. 70

questions.question: What is dialectical materialism in Marxist philosophy?
questions.directAnswer: The philosophy that material economic realities drive history through the clash of opposing class contradictions.
questions.vivaAnswer: Dialectical materialism, developed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, holds that physical, material conditions and economic production—not ideas or spirit—are the foundation of all human reality. History progresses through dialectical contradictions between social classes (thesis and antithesis), culminating in qualitative revolutionary transformation.
keyPoints: Formulated by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
Inverts Hegelian idealism: matter and labor precede consciousness
Class struggle is the historical engine driving systemic change
questions.explanation: Marx famously asserted: 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness.'
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 16-17; Question Bank, p. 55, 56

questions.question: Explain the Marxist model of base and superstructure.
questions.directAnswer: The economic base (forces and relations of production) conditions the cultural superstructure (laws, religion, art, politics).
questions.vivaAnswer: The base-superstructure model is the architectural metaphor of Marxist social theory. The economic 'base' consists of the material means of production and class relations; the 'superstructure' comprises the cultural, political, legal, religious, and artistic institutions that grow out of and legitimize that economic base.
keyPoints: Base (infrastructure): factories, raw materials, labor, capital, class relations
Superstructure: ideology, law, state, philosophy, literature, religion
Economic determinism: economic mode determines cultural forms
Art reflects the ideological conflicts rooted in the material base
questions.explanation: Under industrial capitalism, the private ownership of factories (base) generates laws protecting private property contracts and novels celebrating bourgeois individualism (superstructure).
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 17-18; Question Bank, p. 55, 57

questions.question: What did Friedrich Engels mean by the 'relative autonomy' of art?
questions.directAnswer: That art is ultimately conditioned by the economic base, but possesses independent aesthetic traditions and can critique society.
questions.vivaAnswer: Engels warned against crude economic determinism, insisting that the economic base is the ultimate determinant only 'in the last instance'. The ideological superstructure—especially art and literature—possesses 'relative autonomy', allowing writers to express complex aesthetic traditions, achieve critical distance from their own class, and even expose capitalist contradictions.
keyPoints: Rejection of mechanical, vulgar Marxist determinism
Determination 'in the last instance' by economics
Engels praised Balzac, a conservative monarchist whose realist novels ruthlessly exposed the decay of the French aristocracy
questions.explanation: In his famous letter to Margaret Harkness, Engels stated that he was far from finding fault with her for not writing an overtly propagandistic socialist novel, because genuine art reveals historical truths regardless of the author's personal politics.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 17-18; Question Bank, p. 57

questions.question: What is ideology according to classical Marxist criticism?
questions.directAnswer: The system of ruling-class ideas that presents historical exploitation as natural, inevitable, and universally true.
questions.vivaAnswer: In Marxist theory, ideology is the system of beliefs, values, and representations that represents the sectional economic interests of the ruling class as universal common sense. It produces 'false consciousness' among workers, disguising exploitation and making contingent historical arrangements seem natural and unchangeable.
keyPoints: 'The ideas of the ruling class are in every epoch the ruling ideas' (Marx)
Inverts reality like a camera obscura
Naturalizes class inequality and blinds subordinates to their exploitation
questions.explanation: Ideology functions most effectively when it does not look like ideology at all, but simply appears as 'just the way the world is'.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 18-19; Question Bank, p. 55, 57, 58

questions.question: How does Catherine Belsey argue that classic realist fiction functions ideologically?
questions.directAnswer: By creating an illusion of an unproblematic, transparent world and positioning the reader as a unified, compliant subject.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Critical Practice' (1980), Catherine Belsey argued that the classic realist novel performs ideological work by smoothing over historical contradictions. Its omniscient narrator and seamless plot make bourgeois reality seem transparent, natural, and harmonious, positioning the reader as an autonomous, unified spectator who passively consumes the social order.
keyPoints: Catherine Belsey's 'Critical Practice' (1980)
Realism naturalizes bourgeois common sense through formal closure
Constructs a unified, compliant subject-position for the reader
Hides the linguistic and ideological construction of reality
questions.explanation: Realism discourages critical questioning because its narrative conventions imply that social problems can be happily resolved within the existing capitalist framework (e.g., through moral redemption or marriage).
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 18; Question Bank, p. 58

questions.question: What is commodity fetishism and alienation in Marx's critique of capitalism?
questions.directAnswer: Alienation is the worker's separation from labor and self; commodity fetishism obscures human exploitation by treating market goods as having magical independent value.
questions.vivaAnswer: Alienation (Entfremdung) is the condition where industrial workers lose ownership and control over what they produce, becoming deskilled appendages to machines. Commodity fetishism, described in 'Das Kapital', occurs when social relationships of human labor are obscured, appearing instead as objective, magical economic relationships between inanimate commodities in the market.
keyPoints: Alienation from: product, production act, human species-essence, and community
Commodity fetishism: human social relations perceived as relations between things
Reification (Lukács): turning living human beings into commercial objects
questions.explanation: When we purchase a garment, we see only its brand and price tag; we are blinded to the alienated sweatshop labor that produced it, fetishizing the commodity.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 18-19; Question Bank, p. 55, 56

questions.question: What is Antonio Gramsci's concept of hegemony?
questions.directAnswer: The ruling class's dominance maintained through cultural and moral leadership that manufactures the willing consent of the masses.
questions.vivaAnswer: Antonio Gramsci formulated 'hegemony' in his 'Prison Notebooks' to describe how the ruling class secures and maintains power not primarily through brute physical coercion, but by organizing the spontaneous consent of subordinate classes. Hegemony operates through civil society—schools, church, media, and family—making ruling-class values the accepted 'common sense' of all.
keyPoints: Antonio Gramsci ('Prison Notebooks', 1929–1935)
Rule by consent rather than direct police/military coercion
Operates across civil society (churches, schools, press, culture)
Dominant values internalised as natural 'common sense'
questions.explanation: Because hegemony is never total or permanent, it must be constantly negotiated, defended, and renewed against counter-hegemonic cultural resistance organized by 'organic intellectuals'.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 19-20; Question Bank, p. 56, 58

questions.question: How did Gramsci differentiate between 'direct rule' (coercion) and 'hegemony' (consent)?
questions.directAnswer: 'Direct rule' uses state force and legal punishment; 'hegemony' uses cultural leadership and moral persuasion in civil society.
questions.vivaAnswer: Gramsci distinguished 'direct rule' (dominio), which is exercised by political society through the state apparatus (police, military, courts) to physically enforce order, from 'hegemony' (direzione), which is exercised across civil society (education, media, literature) to build moral and intellectual consensus. A stable capitalist state relies primarily on hegemony, reserving direct coercion for moments of crisis.
keyPoints: Political society: armed forces, courts, prisons -> coercion / force
Civil society: schools, newspapers, religious bodies -> hegemony / consent
Hegemony creates invisible consent; direct rule imposes visible violence
questions.explanation: If a government must use tanks and batons every day, its hegemony has collapsed; true hegemony ensures people obey voluntarily because they believe the system is legitimate.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 19-20; Question Bank, p. 56, 58

questions.question: How does Louis Althusser distinguish between ISA and RSA?
questions.directAnswer: RSAs function primarily by physical force/repression; ISAs function primarily by ideology and consent.
questions.vivaAnswer: Louis Althusser divided state power into two apparatuses: Repressive State Apparatuses (RSAs—the military, police, prisons, courts) which belong to the public domain and enforce order through physical violence; and Ideological State Apparatuses (ISAs—schools, churches, families, literature, media) which belong largely to civil society and secure submission through the internalization of ideology.
keyPoints: Louis Althusser ('Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses', 1970)
RSA: single, centralized, public, operates by physical violence/coercion
ISA: plural, decentralized, private/social, operates by ideology
Education is the dominant ISA in modern industrial capitalism
questions.explanation: Schools act as the primary ISA by teaching children basic skills along with rules of good behavior, respect for authority, and submissiveness to the social division of labor.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 20; Question Bank, p. 56, 57

questions.question: What does Louis Althusser mean by 'interpellation'?
questions.directAnswer: The process by which ideology 'hails' individuals, constituting them into compliant social subjects who imagine they are freely choosing their actions.
questions.vivaAnswer: Interpellation is Althusser's term for the mechanism by which ideology recruits concrete individuals and transforms them into ideological 'subjects'. Using the metaphor of a policeman shouting 'Hey, you there!' on a street, Althusser showed that when the individual turns around, they recognize that the call is addressed to them, instantly stepping into their assigned social and legal identity.
keyPoints: Interpellation = 'hailing' concrete individuals into subjects
Individuals are always-already interpellated by ideology before birth
Creates the illusion of personal autonomy: we feel free precisely when submitting to ideology
questions.explanation: Democratic consumer capitalism interpellates us as 'free citizens' and 'free consumers', making us feel sovereign while locking us into exploitative capitalist structures.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 20; Question Bank, p. 55, 56

questions.question: What is the difference between George Steiner's 'Engelsian' and 'Leninist' Marxist criticism?
questions.directAnswer: 'Engelsian' criticism allows aesthetic freedom and political complexity; 'Leninist' criticism demands strict, dogmatic adherence to the communist party line.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Language and Silence', George Steiner distinguished two strands of Marxist literary criticism. 'Engelsian' criticism, following Engels's letters, is open, nuanced, and tolerant of artistic complexity, recognizing that great art often transcends an author's conservative ideology. 'Leninist' criticism, hardened under Soviet Socialist Realism, is rigid, dogmatic, and prescriptive, demanding that literature serve as a direct party weapon.
keyPoints: George Steiner's classification of Marxist literary approaches
Engelsian: dialetical, respects artistic autonomy, values aesthetic contradictions
Leninist: instrumental, party-line censorship, demands positive socialist heroes
questions.explanation: Engelsian criticism can appreciate non-Marxist masterpieces like Dostoevsky or Balzac; Leninist criticism judges literature strictly on whether it obeys party directives.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 17; Question Bank, p. 57

questions.question: What did Virginia Woolf mean by the 'androgynous mind' in 'A Room of One's Own'?
questions.directAnswer: A creative state of mind that fuses masculine and feminine qualities without self-conscious gender conflict.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'A Room of One's Own' (1929), Virginia Woolf proposed that the greatest creative minds are 'androgynous'—harmoniously integrating both male and female faculties. Borrowing Coleridge's phrase, Woolf argued that an androgynous mind is fully resonant, incandescent, and uninhibited by grievance or gender self-consciousness, allowing artistic genius to flow unobstructed.
keyPoints: Virginia Woolf ('A Room of One's Own', 1929)
Draws on Samuel Taylor Coleridge's notion of the androgynous intellect
Shakespeare as the supreme model of androgynous creativity
Opposed to modern male writing dominated by an aggressive, self-conscious 'I'
questions.explanation: Woolf believed that when an author writes purely as a man or purely as a woman, the writing becomes polemical, brittle, and aesthetically stunted.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 21-22; Question Bank, p. 62, 78

questions.question: Why did Virginia Woolf invent the fictional character of Judith Shakespeare?
questions.directAnswer: To demonstrate that historical lack of money, education, and autonomy—not lack of talent—prevented women from producing great literature.
questions.vivaAnswer: Woolf invented Judith Shakespeare, William Shakespeare's equally gifted imaginary sister, to expose the material oppression of women. While William went to school, learned Latin, and moved to London to act and write, Judith was denied schooling, beaten for refusing an arranged marriage, mocked by theater managers when seeking a career, and eventually committed suicide in despair after becoming pregnant out of wedlock.
keyPoints: Imaginary sister of William Shakespeare of equal poetic genius
Illustrates the material prerequisites for writing: £500 a year and a room of one's own
Demonstrates that patriarchy systematically silenced female creativity
questions.explanation: Woolf showed that female silence across literary history was not a biological deficit, but the violent outcome of economic, educational, and legal disenfranchisement.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 21; Question Bank, p. 62

questions.question: What is Simone de Beauvoir's central thesis regarding Woman as 'The Other'?
questions.directAnswer: Gender is socially constructed ('One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman'), positioning man as Subject and woman as the inessential Other.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'The Second Sex' (1949), Simone de Beauvoir stated: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' She argued that human culture has established Man as the absolute Subject, the universal human norm, while Woman is defined only in negative relation to him as 'the Other'—the secondary, relative, and inessential being.
keyPoints: Simone de Beauvoir ('The Second Sex', 1949)
Foundational distinction between biological sex and social gender
Man = sovereign Subject / default human norm
Woman = the Other / derivative and dependent object
questions.explanation: Beauvoir showed that woman is not naturally passive or submissive; she is carefully trained from infancy by patriarchal society to fulfill the subordinate role of the Other.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 22; Question Bank, p. 62, 63

questions.question: What is Kate Millett's 'Images of Women' criticism in 'Sexual Politics'?
questions.directAnswer: An analysis exposing how male authors depict female characters to justify and perpetuate patriarchal dominance.
questions.vivaAnswer: Kate Millett's 'Sexual Politics' (1969) inaugurated 'Images of Women' criticism by arguing that sex is a pervasive political institution grounded in male supremacy. She examined canonical male writers—such as D.H. Lawrence, Henry Miller, and Norman Mailer—demonstrating how their fictional depictions of women as passive, submissive victims or predatory viragos reinforce patriarchal power structures.
keyPoints: Kate Millett ('Sexual Politics', 1969)
Patriarchy defined as an overarching political institution of male domination
Exposes misogynistic stereotypes and eroticized violence in male literature
Examines 'androtexts' (literature written by men)
questions.explanation: Millett showed that sexual relationships depicted in literature are not purely private or romantic, but micro-political battles reflecting patriarchal hegemony.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 22-23; Question Bank, p. 62, 63, 73

questions.question: What is gynocriticism and how does Elaine Showalter distinguish it from 'feminist critique'?
questions.directAnswer: Feminist critique analyzes women as readers of male texts; gynocriticism investigates women as writers of their own autonomous literature.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Towards a Feminist Poetics' (1979), Elaine Showalter divided feminist literary study into two modes. 'Feminist critique' is an ideological analysis of women as consumers/readers of male-authored literature (androtexts), exposing patriarchal biases. 'Gynocriticism' shifts the focus entirely to women as producers of literature (gynotexts), analyzing female literary traditions, styles, psychology, and genres.
keyPoints: Elaine Showalter ('Towards a Feminist Poetics', 1979)
Feminist critique: woman as reader of male literature (androtexts)
Gynocriticism: woman as writer of female literature (gynotexts)
Establishes a distinctive female literary tradition and canon
questions.explanation: Gynocriticism frees women's literature from being measured against male norms, constructing an autonomous history centered on female experience.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 23; Question Bank, p. 62, 63

questions.question: What are Elaine Showalter's three historical phases of women's writing?
questions.directAnswer: The Feminine phase (imitation), the Feminist phase (protest), and the Female phase (autonomous self-discovery).
questions.vivaAnswer: Showalter traced women's literary history in English through three major phases: 1) the Feminine phase (c. 1840–1880), where women writers imitated male aesthetic standards and used male pseudonyms (e.g., George Eliot); 2) the Feminist phase (c. 1880–1920), where women writers rebelled, protested patriarchal injustice, and demanded equal rights; and 3) the Female phase (1920 onwards), where women rejected male validation, exploring authentic female consciousness and bodily experience.
keyPoints: Feminine Phase (1840–1880): imitation, internalisation of male norms, male pseudonyms
Feminist Phase (1880–1920): protest, advocacy for suffrage, 'New Woman' fiction
Female Phase (1920–present): autonomous female identity, female aesthetic, self-discovery
questions.explanation: This evolutionary trajectory charts women's progression from subservient imitation of male masters to radical political protest, and ultimately to confident cultural self-definition.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 23; Question Bank, p. 62, 63

questions.question: What is 'l'écriture féminine' according to Hélène Cixous?
questions.directAnswer: A fluid, bodily mode of writing that escapes and disrupts phallogocentric patriarchal language.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'The Laugh of the Medusa' (1975), Hélène Cixous introduced 'l'écriture féminine' (feminine writing). She called on women to 'write through the body', producing a subversive, fluid, rhythmic, and nonlinear style of writing that overflows and breaks down rigid patriarchal logic and phallogocentrism.
keyPoints: Hélène Cixous ('The Laugh of the Medusa', 1975)
'Write your self. Your body must be heard'
Opposes phallogocentrism (patriarchal, binary, linear logic)
Uses metaphors of mother's milk, fluid rhythm, and oceanic flow
questions.explanation: Cixous argued that patriarchal language suppresses the female body and sexuality; l'écriture féminine acts as an aesthetic and political liberation that dismantles masculine hierarchies.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 23-24; Question Bank, p. 62, 63

questions.question: How does Julia Kristeva distinguish the 'semiotic' from the 'symbolic'?
questions.directAnswer: The semiotic is the pre-Oedipal, bodily maternal drive (chora); the symbolic is the paternal order of grammar, law, and logic.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Revolution in Poetic Language' (1974), Julia Kristeva posited two dialectical modalities in language: the 'semiotic' (le sémiotique), rooted in the pre-Oedipal maternal body (chora) and expressed through bodily rhythm, tone, and musicality; and the 'symbolic' (le symbolique), associated with the Law of the Father, social rules, and logical grammar. Avant-garde poetic language uses the semiotic to puncture and revolutionize the symbolic.
keyPoints: Semiotic: maternal, bodily, pre-linguistic, rhythmic, instinctual (chora)
Symbolic: paternal, grammatical, logical, patriarchal law and syntax
Poetic language is where the semiotic erupts through the symbolic order
questions.explanation: Kristeva showed that language is never purely abstract and logical; it is constantly recharged by pre-linguistic bodily drives linked to the maternal bond.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 24; Question Bank, p. 62, 63

questions.question: What was Barbara Smith's key contribution in 'Toward a Black Feminist Criticism' (1977)?
questions.directAnswer: Establishing an autonomous Black feminist literary critical framework addressing the simultaneous oppressions of race, gender, class, and sexuality.
questions.vivaAnswer: Barbara Smith's 1977 essay 'Toward a Black Feminist Criticism' is the foundational text of Black feminist literary theory. She argued that Black women writers—such as Toni Morrison, Alice Walker, and Zora Neale Hurston—were completely erased by both white feminist critics (who ignored racism) and Black male critics (who ignored sexism), demanding an autonomous criticism grounded in the interlocking oppressions of race, gender, and class.
keyPoints: Barbara Smith ('Toward a Black Feminist Criticism', 1977)
Exposes white feminism's racism and Black nationalist sexism
Pioneered the intersectional analysis of Black women's literature
Provided a groundbreaking lesbian feminist reading of Toni Morrison's 'Sula'
questions.explanation: Smith proved that Black women writers constitute a rich, distinct literary tradition that cannot be understood through the single-axis lenses of white feminism or male Black nationalism.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 24-25; Question Bank, p. 61, 62

questions.question: How does Audre Lorde's poem 'A Woman Speaks' reflect Black feminist criticism?
questions.directAnswer: By affirming that womanhood and Black racial identity are inseparable, refusing to subordinate either identity.
questions.vivaAnswer: Audre Lorde's poem 'A Woman Speaks' directly enacts Black feminist philosophy. Proclaiming 'Moon marked and touched by sun / my magic is unwritten', the speaker asserts ancestral spiritual power outside white patriarchal textuality, ending with the unequivocal declaration: 'I am / woman / and not white'—insisting that gender and race are indivisible.
keyPoints: Audre Lorde's 'A Woman Speaks'
Combines gender affirmation ('woman') with racial pride ('not white')
Defies the erasure of Black female voices in canonical written traditions
Celebrates female power, cosmic imagery, and self-definition
questions.explanation: Lorde famously warned: 'The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house', asserting that liberation requires honoring differences rather than enforcing white bourgeois uniformity.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 25; Question Bank, p. 83

questions.question: How does Chandra Talpade Mohanty critique Western feminism in 'Under Western Eyes' (1984)?
questions.directAnswer: She attacks Western feminism for constructing an imaginary, homogenized 'Third World Woman' as uniformly helpless, uneducated, and victimized.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Under Western Eyes' (1984), Chandra Talpade Mohanty critiqued Western feminist scholarship for exercising discursive colonialism. Western feminists falsely homogenize women of the Global South into a monolithic, singular category—the 'Third World Woman'—depicting her as universally victimized, uneducated, and tradition-bound, while casting Western women as modern, liberated, and enlightened.
keyPoints: Chandra Talpade Mohanty ('Under Western Eyes', 1984)
Critique of discursive colonialism by Western academic feminists
Deconstructs the monolithic archetype of the 'Third World Woman'
Demands attention to specific material, historical, and class contexts
questions.explanation: Mohanty argued that by treating non-Western women as a passive, homogenous mass, Western feminists replicate imperialist paternalism under the guise of international sisterhood.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 25; Question Bank, p. 61, 64, 73

questions.question: Why does Gayatri Spivak argue that subaltern women are doubly silenced in colonial discourse?
questions.directAnswer: Because they are simultaneously crushed by foreign imperial domination and native patriarchal oppression, leaving no recognized space for their speech.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988), Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak demonstrated that the colonized woman suffers a double marginalization: she is subjugated from above by British colonial power and from within by indigenous patriarchal traditions. When Western legal discourse and native male elites debate female practices (such as sati), the subaltern woman's own subjective voice is completely silenced.
keyPoints: Double colonization: victim of colonial racism and native patriarchy
Spivak's famous formula: 'White men are saving brown women from brown men'
The Hindu widow is an object of ideological debate, never a speaking subject
Epistemic violence erases indigenous female agency
questions.explanation: Spivak's analysis showed that even well-meaning colonial legal reforms served the imperial narrative of moral superiority, rather than empowering Indian women to articulate their own desires.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 25; Question Bank, p. 64, 73

questions.question: Who wrote 'A Room of One's Own' and what is its most famous material requirement for female writing?
questions.directAnswer: Virginia Woolf, who stated that a woman must have £500 a year and a room of her own to write fiction.
questions.vivaAnswer: Virginia Woolf published 'A Room of One's Own' in 1929. Its most famous dictum is that 'a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction', establishing financial autonomy and physical privacy as indispensable material prerequisites for intellectual creation.
keyPoints: Virginia Woolf (1929, based on lectures at Newnham and Girton colleges)
Materialist feminist argument: intellectual freedom depends on material conditions
£500 per year represents financial independence from male breadwinners
A room with a lock represents privacy and uninterrupted concentration
questions.explanation: Woolf stripped away the romantic myth that genius emerges spontaneously regardless of circumstance, demonstrating that centuries of poverty and domestic servitude had silenced female art.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 21; Question Bank, p. 62

questions.question: How does traditional patriarchal mythology construct woman as the Other in fairy tales?
questions.directAnswer: By dividing female characters into extreme archetypes: the passive, pure virgin waiting to be rescued, or the evil, monstrous witch punished for autonomy.
questions.vivaAnswer: Fairy tales exemplify Beauvoir's 'Woman as Other' by polarizing women into rigid stereotypes. Virtuous heroines like Snow White or Cinderella are passive, silent, and beautiful, sleeping or waiting for a male prince (the Subject) to give them identity and status. Independent women with power, like stepmothers and witches, are demonized as unnatural, jealous, and grotesque monsters.
keyPoints: Madonna/whore binary reflected in fairy tales
Passive heroine rewarded with marriage; assertive woman punished as evil
Woman's worth is determined exclusively in relation to male approval
questions.explanation: These childhood narratives socialize young girls into immanence and passivity, reinforcing patriarchal norms from early developmental stages.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 22; Question Bank, p. 62

questions.question: Which male authors did Kate Millett famously critique in 'Sexual Politics'?
questions.directAnswer: D.H. Lawrence, Henry Miller, and Norman Mailer.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'Sexual Politics' (1969), Kate Millett offered scathing close readings of twentieth-century male icons D.H. Lawrence, Henry Miller, and Norman Mailer. She exposed how their celebrated sexual scenes were in reality celebrations of male dominance, sadism, and the humiliation of female characters disguised as spiritual or erotic liberation.
keyPoints: Kate Millett ('Sexual Politics', 1969)
Critiqued D.H. Lawrence's phallic mysticism and demands for female submission
Exposed Henry Miller's casual misogyny and objectification of women
Condemned Norman Mailer's aggressive, macho posturing and sexual violence
questions.explanation: Millett shocked the literary establishment by demonstrating that widely revered 'counter-cultural' male novelists were ardent defenders of patriarchal political supremacy.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 22-23; Question Bank, p. 63, 73

questions.question: Who coined the terms 'androtext' and 'gynotext'?
questions.directAnswer: Elaine Showalter in 'Towards a Feminist Poetics' (1979).
questions.vivaAnswer: Elaine Showalter introduced 'androtext' to denote books written by men, and 'gynotext' to describe books written by women. She argued that gynocriticism must focus its analytical energy on gynotexts to uncover the distinct structures, motifs, and psychological realities of the female literary tradition.
keyPoints: Androtext: text authored by a man
Gynotext: text authored by a woman
Central conceptual tools of gynocriticism
questions.explanation: Showalter wanted feminist critics to stop spending all their time reacting to male misogyny in androtexts and instead build serious scholarly appreciation for gynotexts.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 23; Question Bank, p. 62

questions.question: What is Luce Irigaray's critique of phallogocentrism in 'This Sex Which Is Not One'?
questions.directAnswer: She argues that female sexuality and language are plural and diffuse, resisting the singular, unitary logic of male phallic discourse.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'This Sex Which Is Not One' (1977), French feminist Luce Irigaray critiqued psychoanalysis and philosophy for treating the male organ (the phallus) as the sole standard of sexual value. She argued that female sexuality is plural, auto-erotic, and 'not one', mirrored in the two lips of female anatomy that constantly touch without dominating; feminine language must embrace this multiplicity against linear patriarchal logic.
keyPoints: Luce Irigaray ('This Sex Which Is Not One', 1977)
Critique of Freudian 'penis envy' and male-centered pleasure
Female anatomy and desire as plural, diffuse, and tactile
Challenges singular, linear phallogocentric discourse
questions.explanation: Irigaray showed that Western logic mirrors male unitary sexuality (one tool, one truth, one erection), whereas female desire is reciprocal, continuous, and multifaceted.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 23-24; Question Bank, p. 62, 63

questions.question: What is 'womanism' as formulated by Alice Walker?
questions.directAnswer: A Black feminist commitment to the survival, wholeness, and liberation of an entire people, male and female.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens' (1983), Alice Walker introduced the term 'womanist' as an alternative to mainstream white feminism. Rooted in Black folk speech, a womanist is committed to the survival, spiritual wholeness, and liberation of both women and men in the Black community, famously remarking: 'Womanist is to feminist as purple is to lavender.'
keyPoints: Alice Walker ('In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens', 1983)
Addresses race, gender, class, and culture simultaneously
Affirms solidarity with men in the community against racial oppression
'Womanist is to feminist as purple is to lavender'
questions.explanation: Walker felt 'feminism' was too narrow, middle-class, and white, whereas 'womanism' celebrated the rich artistic resilience and community-wide love of Black women.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 24; Question Bank, p. 61, 62

questions.question: Who coined the critical term 'intersectionality'?
questions.directAnswer: Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989.
questions.vivaAnswer: Legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw coined the term 'intersectionality' in 1989. She used the metaphor of a traffic intersection to show that Black women experience compounded discrimination at the crossroads of race and sex; if an accident occurs in the intersection, it cannot be blamed exclusively on cars coming from one direction.
keyPoints: Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989 legal paper)
Traffic intersection metaphor for overlapping systems of discrimination
Single-axis legal and critical frameworks fail women of color
questions.explanation: Intersectionality became the foundational paradigm across modern feminism, sociolinguistics, and cultural studies for examining overlapping social identities.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 24; Question Bank, p. 61, 62

questions.question: How does postcolonial feminism bridge Third World political activism and Western literary theory?
questions.directAnswer: By applying post-structuralist techniques of deconstruction to dismantle both colonial and patriarchal power structures in global literature.
questions.vivaAnswer: Postcolonial feminism, through scholars like Gayatri Spivak and Chandra Mohanty, merges the rigorous deconstructive methodologies of Derrida and Foucault with anti-imperialist political struggles. It interrogates how Western literary canons marginalize colonized peoples while simultaneously challenging native patriarchal traditions that silence Third World women.
keyPoints: Combines post-structuralist textual critique with material anti-imperialism
Exposes Eurocentric biases in Western literary scholarship
Critiques indigenous patriarchal traditions without justifying colonial intervention
questions.explanation: This framework prevents scholars from falling into either naive Western imperial feminism or reactionary native fundamentalism, demanding nuanced contextual critique.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 25; Question Bank, p. 64, 73

questions.question: How does Sigmund Freud structure the human psyche into Id, Ego, and Superego?
questions.directAnswer: The Id is instinctual (pleasure principle), the Ego is realistic/mediating (reality principle), and the Superego is moral/conscience.
questions.vivaAnswer: Freud structured the psyche into three interacting components: the Id (the primitive, unconscious reservoir of instinctual drives operating on the pleasure principle); the Ego (the realistic mediator between the Id and the external world, operating on the reality principle); and the Superego (the internalized moral conscience and societal values that punishes the Ego with guilt).
keyPoints: Id (das Es): instinctual, amoral, seeks immediate gratification (pleasure principle)
Ego (das Ich): rational, conscious mediator with reality (reality principle)
Superego (das Über-Ich): moral judge, internalized parental and social authority
questions.explanation: Mental health depends on the Ego successfully balancing the violent biological drives of the Id, the punishing perfectionism of the Superego, and the constraints of the external world.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, pp. 26-27; Question Bank, p. 58, 59, 76

questions.question: What is the unconscious in Freudian psychoanalysis and how does it manifest in daily life?
questions.directAnswer: The vast submerged mental realm of repressed desires and memories that erupts through dreams, slips of the tongue, and symptoms.
questions.vivaAnswer: The unconscious is the hidden, dynamic mental domain containing repressed instinctual desires, traumatic memories, and unacceptable fears. Though inaccessible to direct conscious awareness, unconscious impulses constantly exert pressure on waking life, manifesting through parapraxes (Freudian slips of the tongue), jokes, neurotic symptoms, dreams, and works of literature.
keyPoints: Submerged part of the iceberg metaphor (consciousness is merely the tip)
Repressed material remains active, seeking disguised outlets
Manifests in parapraxes (slips of tongue/pen), dreams, and literary symbolism
questions.explanation: Freud emphasized that the conscious mind is not 'master in its own house'; human behavior is fundamentally steered by unconscious motives.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 26; Question Bank, p. 59, 60

questions.question: What is the Oedipus complex according to Freud?
questions.directAnswer: A child's unconscious sexual desire for the opposite-sex parent and aggressive rivalry with the same-sex parent.
questions.vivaAnswer: Named after Sophocles' mythical king Oedipus, the Oedipus complex describes a young boy's unconscious sexual longing for his mother during the phallic stage of psychosexual development, accompanied by murderous hostility toward his rival father. Maturation requires repressing this incestuous wish due to castration anxiety and identifying with the father.
keyPoints: Occurs during phallic stage (ages 3–5)
Incestuous desire for mother + rivalry/death-wish toward father
Castration anxiety leads to repression and paternal identification
Electra complex is Carl Jung's female counterpart
questions.explanation: Successful resolution of the Oedipus complex is foundational for the development of the Superego and normal socialization into the Law of the Father.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 27; Question Bank, p. 58, 82

questions.question: How did Freud and Ernest Jones interpret Hamlet's delay through the Oedipus complex?
questions.directAnswer: Hamlet cannot kill Claudius because Claudius enacted Hamlet's own repressed unconscious desire to kill the father and possess the mother.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'The Interpretation of Dreams' and Ernest Jones's study 'Hamlet and Oedipus' (1949), psychoanalytic critics explained Hamlet's paralysis in avenging his father. Claudius murdered King Hamlet and married Gertrude—precisely what Hamlet's own unconscious Oedipal desire wished to do. Paralyzed by unconscious guilt, Hamlet cannot punish Claudius without confronting his own identical guilt.
keyPoints: Freud in 'The Interpretation of Dreams' (1900); Ernest Jones (1949)
Claudius realizes Hamlet's repressed unconscious Oedipal fantasy
Paralyzing moral self-reproach replaces vengeful action
Explains the play's hesitation and Hamlet's obsession with Gertrude's sexuality
questions.explanation: Hamlet's conscious disgust at his uncle is secretly an unconscious loathing of himself, as Claudius represents Hamlet's own repressed sexual and patricidal wishes.
questions.sourceRef: E403 Study Notes, p. 27; Question Bank, p. 58, 82

questions.question: How does D.H. Lawrence's novel 'Sons and Lovers' depict the Oedipus complex?
questions.directAnswer: Through Paul Morel's consuming, suffocating attachment to his mother Gertrude, which cripples his adult romantic relationships.
questions.vivaAnswer: D.H. Lawrence's 'Sons and Lovers' is a classic literary depiction of the Oedipus complex. Paul Morel shares an intense, emotionally incestuous bond with his mother Gertrude, despising his rough miner father Walter. Unconsciously fixated on his mother, Paul is psychologically incapable of giving himself fully to other women, causing the failure of his relationships with Miriam and Clara.
keyPoints: D.H. Lawrence's autobiographical masterpiece (1913)
